newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak president rejects anti-subversion law.
newsitem.headline: Slovak president rejects anti-subversion law.

text.p: Slovak President Michal Kovac has refused to sign a controversial anti-subversion law criticised as anti-democratic by the European Union and United States, his spokesman said on Thursday.

The law, which borrows heavily from communist-era legislation and was approved by parliament last month, sets out punishments for acts such as organising anti-government demonstrations and other crimes against the state.
"The President returned the law to parliament for revision on the grounds that he considered it politically highly risky," Kovac's spokesman, Vladimir Stefko, told Reuters.
The legislation sparked strong opposition within Slovakia, and drew criticism from Western governments for what is seen as an anti-democratic slant as the country seeks NATO membership.
Both the EU and U.S. issued diplomatic warnings about deficient legislation and government actions which could delay Slovakia's acceptance into the EU and NATO.
Kovac rejected the original version last year, but the ruling coalition of Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar, a bitter enemy of Kovac, moved a new version in parliament in December.
"According to the constitution, parliament must re-discuss the law, once returned by the president," Stefko said.
Parliament can override the president's veto if a simple majority of a quorum present in the 150-member house, where the broad three-party coalition is in control, votes to approve the measure.
"The president has found it unconstitutional that the deputies approved a new, almost identical version, without rejecting the old one," he added.

The law, initiated by the ultra-right Slovak National Party, a junior member of Meciar's coalition, is widely seen as aimed mainly against the activities of Slovakia's 600,000-strong ethnic Hungarian community.
The new version has effectively dropped only one clause from the original which would have made it a crime to spread false information abroad.
The new law also replaced the phrase "organising public rallies" with "calling for mass riots" which, its authors say, conforms to European standards.
Economically motivated strikes are not recognised as mass riots, the law says.
